1. Acute cough and coryzal symptoms:
   - Assessment/likely diagnosis: Viral upper respiratory infection (common cold/nasopharyngitis) — DDx: “High.”
   - Differential diagnosis (consistent with DDx):
     - Influenza — “Medium” likelihood. Supporting: myalgias, headache, chills, acute onset. Opposing: no fever reported; patient not systemically unwell on exam.
     - COVID-19 — “Medium” likelihood. Supporting: cough, myalgias, headache, chills, rhinorrhea. Opposing: no known exposure; no anosmia/ageusia or dyspnea; no test performed.
     - Allergic rhinitis with postnasal drip — “Low” likelihood. Supporting: rhinorrhea, dry cough. Opposing: systemic symptoms (myalgias, chills) favor infection.
     - ACE inhibitor–induced cough (lisinopril) — “Low” likelihood. Supporting: dry cough, current ACE inhibitor use. Opposing: abrupt onset with viral prodrome; longstanding ACE inhibitor use.
   - Investigations planned: None today.
   - Treatment planned:
     - Over-the-counter “Night Nurse/Day Nurse” recommended; clinician confirmed compatibility with current medications.
     - No antibiotics or other prescriptions issued.
     - Safety-net: Contact clinic if shortness of breath, wheeze, or worsening occurs, or if symptoms last >3 weeks; may require in-person chest examination.
   - Relevant referrals: None.
